Canonical phase space

Variables

The dynamical state at arc length $s$ is the six-vector

\[z=(x,\,p_x,\,y,\,p_y,\,l,\,\delta).\]

  • $x,y$: transverse displacements from the reference orbit [m].
  • $p_x=P_x/p_0$, $p_y=P_y/p_0$: canonical momenta normalised to the reference momentum $p_0$.
  • $\delta=(p-p_0)/p_0$: relative momentum deviation.
  • $l=-v(\delta)\,\Delta t$: longitudinal coordinate conjugate to $\delta$, with $\Delta t=t-t_0(s)$ the time lag relative to the reference particle and $v(\delta)$ the particle speed,

\[\frac{v(\delta)}{v_0}=\frac{1+\delta}{\beta_0\sqrt{(1+\delta)^2+1/(\beta_0\gamma_0)^2}}.\]

The reference particle has charge $Ze$, rest energy $mc^2$, Lorentz factor $\gamma_0$, velocity $v_0=\beta_0 c$ and momentum $p_0$.

From $(t,-E)$ to $(l,\delta)$

The $s$-Hamiltonian is first written with the longitudinal pair $(t,-E)$. A type-2 generating function at fixed $s$,

\[F_2(t,\delta;s)=-(t-s/v_0)\,E(\delta)/p_0,\]

produces the new coordinate $l=\partial F_2/\partial\delta=-(t-s/v_0)\,v(\delta)$ and adds $\partial F_2/\partial s=E(\delta)/(p_0 v_0)$ to the Hamiltonian. After dropping a constant, that addition is the energy term $e(\delta)$ below. Because $l$ is conjugate to $\delta$, the momentum deviation $\delta=(p-p_0)/p_0$ is the true relative momentum, not an energy offset.

The symplectic form on this space is the standard one,

\[\omega=\mathrm{d}x\wedge\mathrm{d}p_x+\mathrm{d}y\wedge\mathrm{d}p_y+\mathrm{d}l\wedge\mathrm{d}\delta,\]

or in matrix form $S=\mathrm{diag}(S_2,S_2,S_2)$ with $S_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$. A map $z\mapsto\mathcal{M}(z)$ is symplectic iff its Jacobian satisfies $J^\mathsf{T}SJ=S$.

Output (non-canonical) coordinates

For plots and comparison with laboratory data one uses

\[u=(x,\,x',\,y,\,y',\,\phi,\,\delta),\qquad x'=\frac{p_x}{p_s},\quad p_s=\sqrt{(1+\delta)^2-p_x^2-p_y^2},\quad \phi=-h\omega_0\Delta t=\frac{2\pi h}{C}\,\frac{l}{v(\delta)/v_0}.\]

$\phi>0$ means early arrival. The set $u$ is not canonical: $x'$ depends on $\delta$ and $p_y$, and $\phi$ is scaled by $1/v(\delta)$. Symplecticity is therefore checked only in $z$. The conversion $z\leftrightarrow u$ is exact (nonlinear); truncated polynomial maps apply it as a full Taylor polynomial to the map order.

Energy term

Every magnetic Hamiltonian uses

\[e(\delta)=\frac{1}{\beta_0}\sqrt{(1+\delta)^2+\frac{1}{\beta_0^2\gamma_0^2}}-\frac{1}{\beta_0^2},\]

chosen so that the irrelevant constant vanishes at $\delta=0$ after removal of the constant term of $H$.
